analysis.one_liner: Transfers the U.S. Postal Service to a private corporation, with shares first going to its employees.
analysis.headline: The bill to privatize the Postal Service was introduced by one representative, picked up 4 cosponsors, and died in a House committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have handed the entire United States Postal Service — its buildings, fleet, and routes — to a private corporation. Postal employees would elect the corporation's incorporators and receive its first shares based on seniority, with their retirement benefits kept whole; after one year the shares could be sold to the public. A commission picked by the President would manage the handover, and the President would send Congress a plan to abolish the Postal Service, with a legal mail monopoly kept alive for the new corporation's first five years.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the first winners would have been postal employees, who would receive shares of the new company based on years of service and pay, with retirement benefits guaranteed to match their federal ones. After the first year, the shares could be sold to the general public and investors, who would gain ownership of a mail system carrying the legal protection of the private express statutes for five years — meaning competitors could not deliver letters against it.

how_it_helps.text: Postal employees would have owned the corporation first: for one year its securities could be issued only to Postal Service employees, allocated by years of service and level of pay.
Retirement benefits for employees of the new corporation had to be comparable to what they would have earned as Postal Service employees.

The bill required the new corporation to deliver postal service consistent with the existing universal-service standards of title 39 and to set rates under the existing rate-setting framework, and left the door open to keeping the Postal Rate Commission operating for five years.
A Postal Privatization Commission with seats reserved for employee and management representatives would oversee the issuance of employee securities and consult on the transfer.

analysis.who_pays: The public would give up a public asset: all Postal Service property, rights, liabilities, and obligations would transfer to a private corporation. After the first year, ownership could concentrate among public buyers of the shares, and for five years the new company would keep the legal monopoly on letter delivery — so if a private owner raised postage or scaled back service to unprofitable areas, customers and rural communities would have little recourse beyond whatever rules the President wrote by regulation.

drawbacks.text: The transfer hands all Postal Service assets and liabilities to a private corporation incorporated by as few as nine individuals, and after the first employee-only year the shares could be sold to the public on any terms the corporation chose — so long-term control could end up concentrated far from the workers who received the first shares.

For its first five years the new private corporation would keep the protection of the private express statutes, the legal barrier that blocks competitors from carrying letters — converting a public service obligation into a private monopoly with no guaranteed rate cap beyond proposals the President would develop.

The President would hold broad discretion to write the regulations governing the employee election, the transfer plan, and any other requirements for the corporation, and Congress would only receive a plan and recommendations rather than retain direct control of the process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tries to soften privatization by giving employees the first ownership stake and protecting their pensions, and it keeps the universal-service and rate provisions on paper. But the safeguards are thin: after one year ownership could shift to public investors, the new company keeps a legal monopoly for five years with only proposed rate arrangements, and the whole handover runs through presidential regulation. An honest supporter would have to admit that a service nearly every American relies on, at a uniform price regardless of distance, would be restructured around a private company's bottom line.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee and split between two of its subcommittees, and nothing further happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Philip Crane introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the first day of the 103rd Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, the committee with jurisdiction over the Postal Service.
On January 28, 1993, it was referred to two subcommittees — one handling postal operations and services, the other handling personnel matters — and no further action was ever recorded.
Four Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill sat in committee until the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without a markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Postal Service stayed a public institution and its universal mail service obligations remained in public hands; potential private owners and investors gained nothing. Postal employees and unions that opposed privatization kept the status quo they preferred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public Postal Service and its employees

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to privatize the Postal Service on the first day of the 103rd Congress.

for.name: 4 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the privatization bill; no Democrats joined.

against.name: House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service
against.role: Committee of referral, with jurisdiction over the Postal Service
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; it was split between two subcommittees and no markup or vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Republicans, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled committee before the Congress ended.

industries.note: Privatization would have created a new private owner of the mail system, and the bill proposed keeping the private express statutes — the legal ban on competitors delivering letters — for the new company's first five years. That would have handed a private corporation a protected monopoly over letter delivery, with the risk of higher rates or thinner service paid for by customers.

Employees would have received the first shares of the new company and kept comparable retirement benefits, but they would have become owners of, and workers at, a private firm whose future service obligations and rate rules depended on presidential regulation. Employee ownership is the bill's main concession to ordinary workers.

industries.industry: Public investors in the new postal corporation
industries.note: After the first employee-only year, the corporation's securities could be sold to the general public on terms the corporation itself chose — giving outside investors a chance to own a stake in a legally protected mail monopoly.
